messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean output)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (peak output)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$ (startup time)
        *   $dv \le 0.01\text{ V}$ (stability)
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Operating Conditions (S1-S6): Various loads, excitations, and frequencies.
    *   Reference Design (FBR): Failed ripple, startup, and settled checks. S2 and S4 failed minimum voltage. S3 failed maximum voltage.
    *   Key observation: The open-circuit voltage amplitude is $\sim 3.2\text{ V}$. A standard bridge rectifier (FBR) has diode drops and no regulation, leading to high ripple and potential overvoltage (S3) or undervoltage (S2, S4).

    *   *Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR):* Simple, but high ripple and no voltage control.
    *   *Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE):* Uses a switch to extract charge at the peaks. Very efficient, can potentially boost voltage.
    *   *Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI):* Uses an inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at peaks, increasing the voltage swing and improving efficiency.
    *   *Voltage Clamping:* Using a Zener diode (DZ33) to prevent $v_{max}$ from exceeding 3.6 V.
    *   *Large Storage Capacitor:* To reduce ripple $v_{pp}$ and improve stability $dv$.

    *   *Ripple ($v_{pp} \le 20\text{ mV}$):* Requires a very large output capacitor $C_{out}$.
    *   *Startup ($t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$):* Requires fast energy transfer from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
    *   *Voltage Range ($1.8\text{ V}$ to $3.6\text{ V}$):* S3 creates too much voltage; S4 too little. We need an efficient rectification and possibly a clamp.
    *   *L-Cp Inversion:* The prompt mentions `ton` for L-Cp inversion ($\approx \pi \sqrt{LC_p}$). This hints at SSHI or similar inductive switching.

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI with Full Bridge (Standard SSHI)**
        *   Piezo $\to$ Inductor + Switch (to flip polarity) $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ Storage Cap.
        *   This increases the effective voltage available for rectification.

    *   **Topology 2: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**
        *   Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Rectifier/Cap.
        *   Actually, a simpler SECE: Piezo $C_p$ is charged, then a switch connects it to an inductor and then to the output capacitor.

    *   **Topology 3: Active Rectification / SSHI-lite**
        *   Using the SYNC controller to switch an inductor in parallel with the piezo to flip the voltage, then rectifying the result.

    *   *Design 1: SSHI (Parallel Inductor)*
        *   The piezo is in parallel with a series L-S combination.
        *   The switch S1 closes at the voltage peaks (edges: "both").
        *   The flipped voltage is then rectified by a bridge.
        *   Actually, a simpler version: Piezo $\to$ Bridge $\to$ Cap, but with an L-S flipping circuit across the piezo.
        *   Wait, let's look at the provided components. We have SYNC, S, L, D, C.
        *   Let's try a "Synchronous Switch Harvesting" approach.
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn). Switch (S1) and Inductor (L1) in parallel with the piezo.
        *   Wait, if L1 and S1 are in parallel with the piezo, when S1 closes, the energy in $C_p$ oscillates with $L_1$. After half a cycle ($\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$), S1 opens, and the voltage is inverted.
        *   Then use a full bridge to move the charge to $C_{out}$.

    *   *Design 2: SECE-like (Charge Extraction)*
        *   Piezo is in parallel with $C_p$. A switch S1 connects pzp to an inductor L1, which then connects to a diode D1 and the storage capacitor.
        *   This is more like a boost converter.

    *   *Design 3: FBR with Zener Clamp and Large Capacitor*
        *   Just to see if we can fix the FBR. (Actually, the FBR already failed quite badly on ripple and startup). Let's go for more advanced topologies.

    *   *Refining Design 1 (SSHI):*
        *   Nodes: pzp, pzn, out, 0.
        *   Piezo is across pzp and pzn.
        *   Inductor L1 and Switch S1 are in parallel with the piezo? (S1 nodes [pzp, n1], L1 nodes [n1, pzn]).
        *   Rectifier: D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn].
        *   Storage: C1 [out, 0].
        *   Sync G1: edges="both", ton $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        *   Wait, the standard SSHI puts the L-S flip *before* the rectifier. The bridge then takes the current.
        *   Wait, a simpler SSHI:
            L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn].
            Bridge: D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn].
            C1 [out, 0].

    *   *Refining Design 2 (Synchronous Bridge/Half-Bridge):*
        *   Maybe a "Synchronous Rectifier" using switches?
        *   S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out].
        *   G1: edges="pos", G2: edges="neg".
        *   This replaces the diodes and reduces drop.

    *   *Refining Design 3 (Zener Clamped FBR):*
        *   Bridge as before, but add DZ33 [0, out] to keep $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ and a very large C1 for ripple.
        *   Wait, if I use a Zener, I might solve the $v_{max}$ problem of S3.

    *   Let's focus on the most promising:
        1.  **SSHI (Parallel Inductor + Bridge):** Boosts voltage, improves $t_{up}$ and $v_{avg}$ for S2, S4.
        2.  **Active Rectification (Synchronous switches):** Removes diode drop, helping S2, S4.
        3.  **FBR + Zener + Large C:** Simple baseline to fix S3 and ripple.

    *   Let's double-check the SYNC controller: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
    *   For SSHI: We need the switch to close at the voltage peak. The piezo current is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$. The voltage is $V_p \cos(\omega t)$. Voltage extrema occur at the zero crossings of the current. Perfect.

    *   L-S flipping circuit:
        L1 [pzp, n1]
        S1 [n1, pzn]
        G1 [edges="both"]
    *   Rectifier (Full Bridge):
        D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn]
    *   Storage:
        C1 [out, 0]
    *   Clamp:
        D5 [0, out] (model DZ33) - To protect $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   $L$ value: For $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, if we want $t_{on} \approx 30\text{ $\mu$s}$, $L \approx (t_{on}/\pi)^2 / C_p \approx (10^{-5})^2 / 25\cdot 10^{-9} \approx 4\text{ mH}$.

    *   S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out]
    *   G1: edges="pos", G2: edges="neg"
    *   D1 [0, pzp], D2 [0, pzn] (to provide a path for current when switches are open? No, normally we'd use diodes for the return path).
    *   Wait, the return path is essential. For a half-bridge:
        S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out]
        D1 [0, pzp], D2 [0, pzn]
        C1 [out, 0]
    *   Actually, a full synchronous bridge would need 4 switches. We only have 4 switches total.
    *   Let's try:
        S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out]
        D1 [0, pzp], D2 [0, pzn]
        This is a half-bridge.
        G1: edges="pos", ton=1ms (wide)
        G2: edges="neg", ton=1ms (wide)
        This removes the forward diode drop.

    *   Wait, the standard FBR was:
        D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn].
        C1 [out, 0].
        S3 failed $v_{max}$.
        S2, S4 failed $v_{avg}$.
        Ripple was too high.
        Let's try FBR + DZ33 + Huge C.

    *   `vavg >= 1.8V`, `vmax <= 3.6V`, `vpp <= 0.02V`, `tup <= 0.15s`, `dv <= 0.01V`.
    *   The ripple is the killer. $v_{pp} \le 20\text{ mV}$ is very tight for a $100\text{ Hz}$ source.
    *   $C_{out}$ needs to be large. $I_{load} \approx V/R_L \approx 1.8/330\text{k} \approx 5.4\text{ $\mu$A}$.
    *   $\Delta V = I \cdot \Delta t / C \implies 0.02 = 5.4\text{ $\mu$A} \cdot 0.005\text{ s} / C \implies C \approx 1.3\text{ $\mu$F}$.
    *   Wait, the reference used $2.2\text{ $\mu$F}$ and the ripple was $26\text{ mV}$ (S1). This is close. $20\text{ mV}$ might just require a slightly larger capacitor or better efficiency.

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI-Bridge-Clamp**
        L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 (both), D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn], D5 [0, out] (DZ33), C1 [out, 0].
    *   **Topology 2: Synchronous-Half-Bridge-Clamp**
        S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out], G1 (pos), G2 (neg), D1 [0, pzp], D2 [0, pzn], D3 [0, out] (DZ33), C1 [out, 0].
    *   **Topology 3: FBR-Clamp-HugeC**
        D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn], D5 [0, out] (DZ33), C1 [out, 0].

    *   Actually, Topology 1 is the most sophisticated. Let's refine its values for the proposal.
    *   $L = 4.7\text{ mH}$
    *   $C_{out} = 10\text{ $\mu$F}$ (to be safe on ripple)
    *   $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{4.7\text{m} \cdot 25\text{n}} \approx 34\text{ $\mu$s}$.

    *   Wait, the prompt says "at most 16 components".
    *   Topology 1: L1, S1, G1, D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, C1 = 9 components.
    *   Topology 2: S1, S2, G1, G2, D1, D2, D3, C1 = 8 components.
    *   Topology 3: D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, C1 = 6 components.

    *   Let's double-check the "startup" requirement ($t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$). Large $C_{out}$ *increases* $t_{up}$.
    *   $t_{up} \approx (V_{out} \cdot C_{out}) / P_{avg}$.
    *   For $V_{out}=1.8\text{ V}, C_{out}=10\text{ $\mu$F}, P_{avg}=15\text{ $\mu$W} \implies t_{up} \approx 1.8\cdot 10^{-5} / 15\cdot 10^{-6} \approx 1.2\text{ s}$.
    *   This is too slow! We need $t_{up} \le 0.15\text{ s}$.
    *   So $C_{out}$ cannot be $10\text{ $\mu$F}$.
    *   For $t_{up} = 0.15\text{ s}, C_{out} \approx 0.15 \cdot 15\cdot 10^{-6} / 1.8 \approx 1.25\text{ $\mu$F}$.
    *   This puts us in a tight spot: $C_{out}$ must be large enough for ripple but small enough for startup.
    *   This means we *must* increase the power $P_{avg}$ transferred from the piezo. SSHI is exactly for that.

    *   Let's re-verify SSHI's power: It can significantly increase the harvested power by flipping the voltage, which increases the $dV/dt$ into the storage capacitor.

    *   One more detail: The Zener DZ33. The requirement is $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$. A Zener at $3.3\text{ V}$ will clamp the output. This is good for S3.

    *   Wait, is there a simpler way to get fast startup and low ripple?
        A smaller $C_{out}$ with a voltage regulator? (But we don't have a regulator).
        Or a "Cold Start" circuit? (Not possible with these components).
        Actually, if we use a more efficient harvester (SSHI), $P_{avg}$ increases, allowing a larger $C_{out}$ for the same $t_{up}$.

    *   *Topology 1: SSHI + Bridge + Clamp*
        - L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 (both)
        - D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn] (DSCH)
        - D5 [0, out] (DZ33)
        - C1 [out, 0]
        - Rationale: SSHI increases power for faster startup and higher $v_{avg}$. Bridge rectifies. Zener clamps $v_{max}$. Large $C_{out}$ reduces ripple.

    *   *Topology 2: SECE-like (Single switch boost)*
        - S1 [pzp, n1], L1 [n1, out], D1 [out, n1] (Wait, this is not right).
        - Let's try a simpler SECE:
          S1 [pzp, n1], L1 [n1, n2], D1 [n2, out]
          G1 (pos)
          This extracts charge at the peak.
        - Let's stick to the Synchronous Half-Bridge for the second proposal.

    *   *Topology 3: Modified FBR*
        - D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn] (DSCH)
        - D5 [0, out] (DZ33)
        - C1 [out, 0]
        - Rationale: Use a Zener and a carefully chosen $C_{out}$ to balance ripple and startup.

    *   S1: pzp -> n1 (L1), n1 -> pzn (S1), G1(both)
    *   D1: pzp -> out, D2: pzn -> out, D3: 0 -> pzp, D4: 0 -> pzn
    *   D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
    *   C1: out -> 0

    Wait, if S1 and L1 are in parallel with the piezo, when S1 closes, $C_p$ and $L_1$ form a resonant tank. The voltage flips. This is the classic SSHI. The diodes then rectify this.

    Actually, a better SSHI:
    The bridge is connected to the piezo. The L-S flip is *across* the piezo.
    Wait, that's exactly what I wrote.
    Diodes:
    D1 [pzp, out]
    D2 [pzn, out]
    D3 [0, pzp]
    D4 [0, pzn]
    When $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + V_{diode}$, D1 conducts.
    When $V_{pzn} > V_{out} + V_{diode}$, D2 conducts.
    When $V_{pzp} < -V_{diode}$, D3 conducts.
    When $V_{pzn} < -V_{diode}$, D4 conducts.
    This is a standard bridge.
    The L-S circuit:
    L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn]
    When S1 closes, $V_{pzp}$ and $V_{pzn}$ are shorted through $L_1$.

    *   L: 4.7 mH
    *   C: 2.2 uF
    *   ton: 34 us (for $C_p=25\text{nF}$)
    *   Diodes: DSCH
    *   Clamp: DZ33

    S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out], G1 (pos), G2 (neg), D1 [0, pzp], D2 [0, pzn], D3 [0, out] (DZ33), C1 [out, 0].
    This eliminates the bridge drop.

    Wait, let's check the components: "at most 16 components". "at most 4 switches". "at most 2 SYNC".
    Topology 2 uses 2 switches and 2 SYNCs. This is allowed.
